1	\begin{abstract}
2	Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models encode observations as hundreds of vision tokens, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet its effect varies dramatically across architectures: at retention ratio $k{=}0.95$, $\pi_{0.5}$ preserves 98\% task success while SmolVLA collapses to 0\%---why?
3	
4	We identify the vision-language connector as the strongest architectural predictor of pruning tolerance. The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in a single forward pass, predicts compressibility across the full architecture spectrum: from CV$\,{=}\,$0.038 (near-immune linear projection) to CV$\,{=}\,$0.314 (catastrophic pixel-shuffle collapse). Across six VLA architectures (450\,M--7\,B parameters) and four LIBERO manipulation suites, token-independent connectors degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors exhibit abrupt cliffs: SmolVLA collapses when just 6 of 128 tokens are removed.
5	
6	Importance-based selection is not universally beneficial---it can be actively harmful. L2 norm selection preserves 98\% success on $\pi_{0.5}$ where random yields 5\% (93\,pp gap); at aggressive ratios, random outperforms L2 by up to 36\,pp. No scoring method is universally safe: task complexity amplifies connector-dependent patterns (up to $20{\times}$ from Object to Goal at $k{=}0.9$). A zero-mask ablation isolates the mechanism: zeroing 10\% of tokens preserves 98.0\% SR while physical removal collapses to 9.0\%---the 89\,pp gap is entirely attributable to position disruption, not information loss. For architectures where all deletion fails, a lightweight re-encoding module (${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers $>$60\% success at 75\% compression.
7	\end{abstract}

tool_args.new_string: $\pi_{0.5}$'s random pruning at $k{=}0.9$ collapses to 9.0\% on Object despite removing only 10\% of tokens. We compare hard pruning (removes tokens, re-indexes positions) with zero-masking (zeros embeddings, preserves positions): zero-masking preserves 98.0\% SR while hard pruning collapses to 9.0\%. On $\pi_{0.5}$, the 89\,pp gap is entirely attributable to position disruption: its linear connector tolerates complete signal destruction but not index shifts. This ablation targets $\pi_{0.5}$ specifically because its RoPE-based position encoding makes it most susceptible to re-indexing; other connectors use different positional mechanisms where this dissociation may not hold.

tool_args.old_string:
CV predicts connector-level compressibility, but task complexity determines \emph{which} scoring method succeeds within a given connector---L2 leads on $\pi_{0.5}$ Object but inverts on Long; on X-VLA, attention recovers near-baseline while L2 is anti-informative (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). The V-shaped random recovery on $\pi_{0.5}$ Long reflects position encoding sensitivity: scattered gaps maximally disrupt RoPE at $k{\approx}0.9$, recovering as surviving positions become approximately uniform.

Connector architecture is the strongest predictor of VLA token compressibility. Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully; entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs amplified by task complexity (up to $20{\times}$ from Object to Goal at $k{=}0.9$). CV partitions models in a single forward pass. Under sufficient compression, scoring effectiveness becomes connector- and $k$-dependent. Where all deletion fails, VTR recovers over 60\% SR at 75\% compression. Real-robot validation and adaptive per-task pruning schedules remain open. Code and evaluation scripts will be released upon publication.
tool_args.new_string: Connector architecture is the strongest predictor of VLA token compressibility. Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully; entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs amplified by task complexity (up to $20{\times}$ from Object to Goal at $k{=}0.9$). CV partitions models in a single forward pass; task complexity then determines which scoring method succeeds---L2 leads on $\pi_{0.5}$ Object but inverts on Long, while attention recovers near-baseline on X-VLA but not $\pi_{0.5}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). Where all deletion fails, VTR recovers over 60\% SR at 75\% compression. Real-robot validation and adaptive per-task pruning schedules remain open.

tool_args.old_string: All evaluations use LIBERO simulation; no sim-to-real evidence is provided; real-robot evaluation with domain shift would strengthen practical applicability. The six architectures differ in backbone, encoder, and scale beyond the connector, preventing full causal isolation of the connector effect; controlled studies varying only the connector within a fixed backbone would sharpen causal claims. The CV--SR correlation relies on four closed-loop models, too few for a general law; expanding the model pool as new VLA architectures emerge will test whether CV generalizes as a universal diagnostic. VTR is validated on SmolVLA only; extending to other entangling connectors (e.g., cross-attention encoders) would test generality of the re-encoding approach. Only L2-norm and random scoring are systematically compared; gradient-based importance scoring or learned pruning masks could yield better token selection. Most conditions use a single seed; $\pi_{0.5}$ Long uses five-seed means ($n{=}5$, s.d.\ ${\leq}$2.7\,pp); future work should adopt multi-seed evaluation across all conditions to quantify variance. \textbf{AI disclosure:} This work used AI tools (Claude) for code development and manuscript drafting; all scientific claims are the authors' own.

tool_args.old_string:
Remove 5\% of vision tokens from SmolVLA and its success rate collapses from 59.2\% to near-zero (${\leq}$6.6\%). Apply the same reduction to $\pi_{0.5}$ and it retains 98.2\% under L2 norm selection. Both are Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models built on a ViT encoder feeding tokens through a connector into a language model backbone; the critical difference is the connector architecture. Token pruning is well-established for ViTs~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit,bolya2023tome,liang2022evit} and extends to VLAs~\cite{cheng2026vlaiap,xu2025vlacache,yang2025efficientvla,liu2025vlapruner}, but each method validates on a single architecture, implicitly assuming pruning transfers across designs.

Yet current VLAs employ fundamentally different vision connectors---linear projections~\cite{black2024pi0}, MLP projectors~\cite{kim2024openvla}, pixel-shuffle folding~\cite{shukor2025smolvla}, and learned encoders with cross-token self-attention~\cite{zheng2025xvla}---each imposing distinct constraints on how visual information distributes across tokens. Deploying a pruning method validated on one connector type to another risks silent degradation or complete failure.

We present an empirical study of VLA token compressibility across six architectures (450M--7B) and four LIBERO manipulation suites, identifying the vision-language connector as the strongest predictor of pruning robustness (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}). Three findings emerge:

\emph{First, connector architecture governs the degradation pattern.} Token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully under pruning, while token-entangling connectors (BART encoders, pixel-shuffle) produce catastrophic cliffs---and task complexity amplifies the gap by up to $20{\times}$.

\emph{Second, no scoring method is universally safe.} L2 norm selection can dramatically outperform random pruning on one architecture yet \emph{reverse} on another; the advantage follows an inverted-U curve that peaks at moderate compression and collapses at aggressive ratios. Which method helps---or harms---depends on the connector's token information structure.

\emph{Third, a zero-cost diagnostic predicts these behaviors.} The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token L2 norms, computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes and predicts both pruning tolerance and the threshold at which scoring method choice becomes critical. For architectures where all deletion fails, a lightweight Vision Token Re-encoder (VTR, ${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers over 60\% success rate at 75\% compression.

Our contributions are: (1)~the first cross-architecture compressibility analysis of VLA token pruning, revealing connector type as the dominant factor; (2)~CV as a single-pass diagnostic that predicts pruning tolerance and scoring method sensitivity; and (3)~mechanistic evidence that position disruption---not information loss---drives pruning failure in low-CV architectures, plus VTR as a recovery path for entangling connectors.
tool_args.new_string:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process robot observations as hundreds of vision tokens, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time control. Token pruning---removing low-importance tokens before the language backbone---is well-established for vision transformers~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit,bolya2023tome,liang2022evit} and has been applied to VLAs~\cite{cheng2026vlaiap,xu2025vlacache,yang2025efficientvla,liu2025vlapruner}. Yet each method validates on a single architecture, implicitly assuming that pruning transfers across designs.

This assumption is unsafe. Current VLAs employ fundamentally different vision connectors---linear projections~\cite{black2024pi0}, MLP projectors~\cite{kim2024openvla}, pixel-shuffle folding~\cite{shukor2025smolvla}, and learned encoders with cross-token self-attention~\cite{zheng2025xvla}---each imposing distinct constraints on how visual information distributes across tokens. Whether a pruning strategy validated on one connector type will transfer to another is unknown; deploying it blindly risks silent degradation or complete failure.

We present the first cross-architecture study of VLA token compressibility, evaluating six architectures (450M--7B) across four LIBERO manipulation suites (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}). The vision-language connector emerges as the strongest predictor of pruning robustness: token-independent connectors degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs that task complexity amplifies. No scoring method is universally safe---importance-based selection can dramatically outperform or underperform random pruning depending on the connector, following an inverted-U importance margin that reverses at aggressive compression ratios. A zero-mask ablation isolates the mechanism: position disruption, not information loss, drives failure.

Our contributions: (1)~the first cross-architecture VLA compressibility analysis, revealing connector type as the dominant factor governing pruning tolerance; (2)~the coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms as a zero-cost, single-pass diagnostic predicting both pruning tolerance and scoring method sensitivity; (3)~mechanistic evidence that position disruption drives failure in position-sensitive architectures, plus a lightweight Vision Token Re-encoder (VTR, ${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovering baseline performance at 75\% compression for architectures where all deletion fails.

We set out to understand why identical token pruning produces dramatically different outcomes across VLA architectures. The vision-language connector emerges as the strongest predictor: its coefficient of variation (CV), computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes without task evaluation. Token-independent connectors permit graceful degradation while entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs that task complexity amplifies (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). The importance margin between scoring methods follows an inverted-U curve---no method is universally safe across connectors or tasks---and a zero-mask ablation reveals that position disruption, not information loss, is the binding constraint in position-sensitive architectures. For connectors where all deletion fails, VTR recovers baseline performance at 75\% compression with ${\sim}$5\% additional parameters.

These results provide actionable guidance: evaluate CV before deploying any pruning strategy, and prefer learned re-encoding over deletion for high-CV architectures. Real-robot validation and adaptive per-task compression schedules remain important open directions.
